course.title: Russian: Foundations
course.description: A beginner's introduction to the Russian language, taught entirely in English: what Russian is and where it is spoken, the full Cyrillic alphabet, pronunciation and word stress, grammatical gender and the case system, present-tense verbs, numbers, and everyday phrases. The grammar, vocabulary, and background are drawn from the open article on the Russian language in Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia (CC BY-SA 4.0). The course closes by looking at Russian as a gateway to one of the world's great literary traditions.

questions.prompt: Which alphabet is used to write Russian?
questions.explanation: Russian is written in the Cyrillic alphabet, which grew out of the Greek script - see 'What Russian is and the Cyrillic alphabet'.

questions.prompt: Roughly how many letters are in the modern Russian alphabet?
questions.explanation: The modern Russian alphabet has 33 letters, including two signs that carry no sound of their own.

questions.prompt: The Russian letter В looks like a Latin B but is actually pronounced like...
questions.explanation: В (transliterated v) sounds like English v. It is a classic 'false friend' that looks Latin but sounds different.

questions.prompt: Russian nouns change their endings to show their role in a sentence. This system of endings is called the system of...
questions.explanation: A noun's case ending marks its job (subject, object, and so on) - see 'Nouns, gender, and the case system'.

questions.prompt: How many grammatical genders do Russian nouns have?
questions.explanation: Russian nouns are masculine, feminine, or neuter - three genders, usually recognizable from the ending.

questions.prompt: The polite Russian greeting Здравствуйте (zdravstvuyte) means...
questions.explanation: Здравствуйте (zdravstvuyte) is the polite way to say hello to a stranger or an elder.

questions.prompt: In Russian, the vowel о when it is NOT stressed is usually pronounced...
questions.explanation: This is called vowel reduction: an unstressed о weakens toward an 'a' sound, so молоко (moloko, milk) sounds like 'ma-la-KO'.

questions.prompt: Russian is the native language of celebrated writers such as...
questions.explanation: Tolstoy and Dostoevsky wrote in Russian; reading them in the original is a major reason learners study the language.

lessons.title: What Russian is and the Cyrillic alphabet
lessons.grammar_note: Russian is written in Cyrillic, a largely phonetic script of 33 letters; several letters look like Latin letters but stand for entirely different sounds.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: By the end of this lesson you will be able to say what the Russian language is, name several places where it is spoken, recognize the Cyrillic alphabet, and read the letters that look like Latin letters but sound completely different. Warm-up: the Russian word for 'yes' is written да and sounds like 'da' - which of those two letters do you think you could already read? Russian is written in Cyrillic, a script that can look intimidating at first glance. The good news is that Cyrillic is highly phonetic: once you learn the sound of each letter, you can sound out almost any word, because the letters behave far more predictably than English spelling does. This lesson gives you the whole alphabet at once, so that every later lesson can show you real Russian words without leaving you stranded. Keep this page handy and the shapes will start to feel familiar faster than you expect.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Russian is an East Slavic language and the most widely spoken Slavic language in the world. It is the official language of Russia and is used across much of the former Soviet Union, including in countries such as Belarus, Kazakhstan, and Kyrgyzstan, and it is one of the official working languages of the United Nations. Hundreds of millions of people speak it as a first or second language, which makes it one of the most studied languages on earth. People learn Russian for science, diplomacy, trade, travel, and, as this course stresses at the end, for direct access to a towering literary tradition. Russian is written with the Cyrillic alphabet, which has 33 letters. Cyrillic grew out of the Greek alphabet and was developed to write Slavic languages more than a thousand years ago. Unlike English, Russian spelling is largely phonetic, so the letters reliably tell you how to pronounce a word. Learning the alphabet is therefore the single most valuable first step you can take.

sections.heading: Key words & examples
sections.text: Here is the whole alphabet, with each letter, its name, and its sound. А (ah) as in father; Б (beh) like b; В (veh) like v; Г (geh) like hard g in go; Д (deh) like d; Е (yeh) like ye in yes; Ё (yo) like yo in yonder; Ж (zheh) like s in measure; З (zeh) like z; И (ee) like ee in see; Й (short i) like y in boy; К (kah) like k; Л (el) like l; М (em) like m; Н (en) like n; О (oh) like o; П (peh) like p; Р (er) a rolled r; С (es) like s; Т (teh) like t; У (oo) like oo in boot; Ф (ef) like f; Х (khah) like ch in Scottish loch; Ц (tseh) like ts in cats; Ч (cheh) like ch in church; Ш (shah) like sh; Щ (shchah) a longer, softer sh; Ъ (hard sign) no sound of its own; Ы (yery) a hard 'i' made at the back of the mouth; Ь (soft sign) no sound of its own; Э (eh) like e in met; Ю (yoo) like you; Я (yah) like ya in yard. Say each name aloud as you point to its letter.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: The trickiest letters are the ones that look like Latin letters but sound different - the false friends. Try reading these, then check the answers. 1) The letter В - does it sound like English b or v? 2) The letter Р - is it an English p or something else? 3) The letter Н - is it an h or an n? 4) The letter С - is it a k sound or an s sound? 5) The letter У - does it sound like English y or oo? 6) Read the word ресторан (restoran). What everyday place is it? Answers: 1) like v, so В is a false friend for b. 2) it is a rolled r, not a p. 3) it is n, not h. 4) it is always an s sound, like the s in sit. 5) it sounds like oo, as in boot. 6) 'restaurant' - once you trust the sounds, the word reads itself.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: reading Cyrillic letters as if they were Latin - seeing Р and saying 'p', or Н and saying 'h'. Train your eye to treat each shape as its true Russian sound. Mistake: skipping the two signs, Ъ and Ь; they carry no sound of their own, but they change the consonant before them, so they matter. Mistake: confusing И (ee) with Й (short i, a y sound); the small hook on top changes everything. Mistake: trying to memorize all 33 letters in one sitting - space your practice over several short sessions instead. Exit ticket: (a) How many letters are in the Russian alphabet? (b) What sound does В make? (c) Does the letter Р sound like English p? Answers: 33 letters; the sound of English v; no, it is a rolled r. Keep a copy of the alphabet nearby for the next few lessons.

lessons.title: Pronunciation, vowel reduction, and word stress
lessons.grammar_note: Russian has one strong stress per word, and unstressed vowels - especially о - are reduced, so where the stress falls changes how a word sounds.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: By the end of this lesson you will be able to find the stressed syllable in a Russian word, pronounce unstressed vowels correctly through a process called vowel reduction, and understand why the same letter can sound different depending on where the stress falls. Warm-up: the word for 'milk' is молоко (moloko), but it is actually pronounced closer to 'ma-la-KO'. Can you guess which syllable is stressed? Russian pronunciation rewards attention to stress more than almost anything else. Unlike the predictable stress of some languages, Russian stress can fall on any syllable and is not marked in ordinary writing, so learners simply have to learn it word by word. The payoff is large: once you place the stress correctly, the vowels fall into place and your speech sounds far more natural to a Russian ear.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Every Russian word of more than one syllable has exactly one stressed syllable, and that syllable is pronounced long and clear. The catch is that stress is free - it can land anywhere - and it is not written, so you learn it together with each new word. Stress drives a second feature called vowel reduction. When the vowel о is unstressed, it is not pronounced as a full 'o'; instead it weakens toward an 'a' sound, and further from the stress it fades toward a neutral 'uh'. The vowel е, when unstressed, drifts toward a short 'i' sound. So молоко (moloko, milk) is really said 'ma-la-KO', with only the final stressed о sounding like a clear 'o'. This is why listening and repeating matter so much: the spelling keeps the letter о, but the sound changes with the stress. Get the stress right and the reduction follows naturally.

sections.heading: Key words & examples
sections.text: Here are words that show stress and reduction. хорошо (khorosho, good or well) is said 'kha-ra-SHO', stress on the last syllable, the first two о's reduced. молоко (moloko, milk) is 'ma-la-KO'. вода (voda, water) is 'va-DA', the unstressed о sounding like 'a'. спасибо (spasibo, thank you) is 'spa-SEE-ba', stress in the middle and the final о reduced to 'a'. окно (okno, window) is 'ak-NO'. Compare стол (stol, table), a one-syllable word where the о stays a full 'o' because it is stressed. Notice the pattern: a stressed о is a clear 'o', while an unstressed о slides toward 'a' or a soft 'uh'. The vowel я, when unstressed, also softens, as in язык (yazyk, language or tongue), said 'yi-ZYK'. Say each word slowly, exaggerating the stressed syllable, then speed up.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Mark the stress and say each word, then check. 1) Where is the stress in спасибо (spasibo)? 2) How is the first о in молоко (moloko) pronounced? 3) In вода (voda), does the о sound like 'o' or 'a'? 4) Does the о in the one-syllable word стол (stol) reduce? 5) What happens to an unstressed е in Russian? Answers: 1) on the middle syllable, 'spa-SEE-ba'. 2) it reduces toward 'a', giving 'ma'. 3) like 'a', because it is unstressed, so 'va-DA'. 4) no - it is the only syllable and it is stressed, so it stays a full 'o'. 5) it drifts toward a short 'i' sound. When in doubt, find the stress first, then let every other vowel relax toward a neutral sound.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: giving every о a full 'o' sound; in Russian only the stressed о is a clear 'o', and the rest reduce. Mistake: guessing stress and moving on; because stress is unmarked and free, it is worth learning deliberately with each word. Mistake: stressing two syllables in one word - Russian words have a single main stress. Mistake: ignoring reduction when you listen, then being surprised that молоко does not sound like its spelling. Exit ticket: (a) How many stressed syllables does a Russian word have? (b) How is an unstressed о pronounced? (c) Is word stress shown in ordinary Russian writing? Answers: exactly one; it reduces toward an 'a' or neutral sound; no, it is not marked, so you learn it with each word.

items.example: Здравствуйте! (zdravstvuyte - Hello! said to a stranger or an elder)
Привет! (privet - Hi! said to a friend)
Спасибо большое. (spasibo bolshoye - Thank you very much.)
Пожалуйста. (pozhaluysta - Please, or You are welcome.)
Да, конечно. (da, konechno - Yes, of course.)
Нет, спасибо. (net, spasibo - No, thank you.)

items.translation: kak dela - How are you? (How are things?)
items.example: Как дела? (kak dela - How are you doing?)
Извините, пожалуйста. (izvinite, pozhaluysta - Excuse me, please.)

lessons.title: Hard and soft consonants, and the soft sign
lessons.grammar_note: Most Russian consonants come in hard and soft pairs; a following soft vowel or the soft sign (ь) softens the consonant, and that can change the word.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: By the end of this lesson you will be able to explain what hard and soft consonants are, hear the difference between them, and recognize how the soft sign (ь) and certain vowels make a consonant soft. Warm-up: say the 'n' in English 'onion' - that little 'ny' glide is close to a Russian soft consonant. Can you feel where your tongue goes? Softness, or palatalization, is one of the features that gives Russian its characteristic sound. It can feel subtle to English speakers at first, but it is not optional: softening a consonant can change one word into another. This lesson keeps things practical, teaching you to notice softness and to read the letters that signal it, rather than drilling every pair at once. Aim for recognition first, and production will follow with listening and practice.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Most Russian consonants exist in two versions: hard (plain) and soft (palatalized). A soft consonant is made by raising the middle of the tongue toward the roof of the mouth, adding a faint 'y' quality, a bit like the start of 'yes'. What tells you a consonant is soft? Two things. First, the vowels я, е, ё, и, and ю after a consonant soften it, while а, э, о, ы, and у keep it hard. Second, the soft sign ь, which has no sound of its own, softens the consonant right before it. There is also a hard sign ъ, much rarer, which keeps a consonant hard and separates it from a following soft vowel. Softness matters because it can distinguish words: мат (mat) with a hard t is one word, while мать (mat, mother) ends in a soft t. Learning to hear and mark softness is a steady, long-term part of learning Russian.

sections.heading: Key words & examples
sections.text: Compare hard and soft. мат (mat), with a hard t, is a flat, plain ending, while мать (mat, mother) ends in a soft t marked by the soft sign ь. Listen for the faint 'y' glide at the end of the soft version. The vowels that soften a preceding consonant appear in нет (net, no), where the е softens the n, and in тётя (tyotya, aunt), where ё and я both soften. Compare лук (luk, onion), with a hard l, and любовь (lyubov, love), where ю softens the l into a 'ly' sound and the final ь softens the v. The word день (den, day) ends in a soft n marked by ь. The word семья (semya, family) uses the soft sign in the middle to separate and soften. Say each pair slowly, listening for the gentle 'y' colour that marks the soft member.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Answer or read, then check. 1) Which sign softens the consonant before it but has no sound of its own? 2) Does the vowel я soften or harden the consonant before it? 3) In мать (mat, mother), is the final t hard or soft? 4) Does the vowel о soften a preceding consonant? 5) What faint sound quality marks a soft consonant? Answers: 1) the soft sign, ь. 2) it softens it, like е, ё, и, and ю. 3) soft, because of the soft sign ь. 4) no - о, а, э, ы, and у keep the consonant hard. 5) a slight 'y' glide, as at the start of 'yes'. If you listen for that glide, you will begin to hear softness even before you can produce it reliably.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: ignoring the soft sign because it has no sound of its own; it still changes the consonant and sometimes the meaning, so мать is not the same as мат. Mistake: treating all vowels alike - remember that я, е, ё, и, and ю soften, while а, э, о, ы, and у keep things hard. Mistake: over-softening at first; aim for a light 'y' colour, not a full separate 'y' syllable. Mistake: confusing the soft sign ь with the rarer hard sign ъ. Exit ticket: (a) Which sign softens the consonant before it? (b) Name two vowels that soften a preceding consonant. (c) Does о soften or harden the consonant before it? Answers: the soft sign ь; any two of я, е, ё, и, ю; it keeps it hard.

lessons.title: Nouns, gender, and the case system
lessons.grammar_note: Russian nouns have one of three genders and change their endings by case; the ending, not the word order, shows a noun's job in the sentence.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: By the end of this lesson you will be able to tell a noun's gender from its ending in most cases, explain what grammatical case is, and understand why Russian noun endings change from one sentence to the next. Warm-up: in English we say 'the dog sees the cat' and rely on word order - but what if the words could carry little tags showing who does what? Russian does exactly that. This is often the moment when Russian grammar clicks or frustrates, so we will go slowly and aim for understanding rather than memorizing every ending. The goal here is to see the logic of gender and case clearly, so that the detailed endings you meet later feel like variations on a pattern you already grasp, not a wall of new forms.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Every Russian noun has a grammatical gender: masculine, feminine, or neuter. You can usually tell gender from the ending of the basic, dictionary form. Nouns ending in a consonant are generally masculine, such as стол (stol, table). Nouns ending in -а or -я are generally feminine, such as вода (voda, water). Nouns ending in -о or -е are generally neuter, such as окно (okno, window). Russian also has grammatical case: nouns change their endings to show their job in a sentence. The main case, the nominative, marks the subject. The accusative marks the direct object. There are six cases in all - nominative, accusative, genitive, dative, instrumental, and prepositional - each with its own set of endings. Because the ending carries the grammar, word order in Russian is flexible, much freer than in English. You do not need every ending today; you need the idea that endings, not position, do the real work.

sections.heading: Key words & examples
sections.text: Gender by ending: стол (stol, table) ends in a consonant, so it is masculine; книга (kniga, book) ends in -а, so it is feminine; окно (okno, window) ends in -о, so it is neuter. Now case. In Это книга (eto kniga, This is a book), книга is in the nominative, the dictionary form, as the subject. In Я читаю книгу (ya chitayu knigu, I am reading a book), the same noun becomes книгу, with the accusative ending -у, because it is now the direct object. The subject Я (ya, I) does not change. Compare Я вижу стол (ya vizhu stol, I see a table): стол, a masculine noun naming a non-living thing, keeps the same form in the accusative. These small ending changes are the heart of Russian grammar, and they let the words move around without confusion.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Answer, then check. 1) What gender is a noun ending in a consonant, such as стол (stol, table)? 2) What gender is книга (kniga, book)? 3) What gender is окно (okno, window)? 4) In Я читаю книгу (ya chitayu knigu), why does книга become книгу? 5) How many cases does Russian have? Answers: 1) usually masculine. 2) feminine, because it ends in -а. 3) neuter, because it ends in -о. 4) because it is the direct object, so it takes the accusative ending -у. 5) six cases in all. If you can name a noun's gender and spot when it is the subject or the object, you already understand the engine of the case system.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: assuming the first noun in a sentence is the subject; in Russian the ending, not the position, marks the subject, so always read the endings. Mistake: forgetting that -а and -я usually signal feminine, not masculine. Mistake: expecting every noun to change in the accusative - masculine nouns for non-living things often look the same as their nominative. Mistake: trying to memorize all six cases at once; learn the nominative and accusative well first. Exit ticket: (a) What gender is a noun ending in -о, such as окно? (b) Which case marks the subject? (c) How many cases does Russian have? Answers: neuter; the nominative; six. Treat case as a system of signposts, and the endings become meaningful rather than random.

questions.prompt: The Russian letter Н is pronounced like...
questions.explanation: Н is a false friend: it looks like an H but is pronounced like English n.

questions.prompt: In Russian, an unstressed о is usually pronounced...
options: the same as a stressed o
questions.explanation: Vowel reduction weakens an unstressed о toward an 'a' sound, so вода (voda) is said 'va-DA'.

questions.prompt: The soft sign (ь) is used to...
questions.explanation: The soft sign has no sound of its own; it softens (palatalizes) the consonant that precedes it, as in день (den, day).

questions.prompt: A Russian noun ending in -а or -я is usually...
questions.explanation: Nouns ending in -а or -я are generally feminine, such as книга (kniga, book).

questions.prompt: How many grammatical cases does Russian have?
questions.explanation: Russian has six cases: nominative, accusative, genitive, dative, instrumental, and prepositional.
Спасибо (spasibo) means thank you; пожалуйста (pozhaluysta) means please or you are welcome.

lessons.title: Verbs, person, and present-tense endings
lessons.grammar_note: A Russian present-tense verb ending shows the person and number of the subject, so the pronoun is often optional.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: By the end of this lesson you will be able to conjugate a regular Russian verb in the present tense, read the ending to tell who the subject is, and understand why Russian often drops the pronoun. Warm-up: if читаю (chitayu) means 'I read', what might читают (chitayut) mean? The ending holds the clue. Russian verbs change their endings for each person, much as the nouns changed for each case, and the pattern is wonderfully regular for the most common verbs. Learning one set of endings lets you handle a whole family of verbs at once. We will use everyday verbs so that the endings attach to words you will actually want to say, rather than to abstract examples you will never use in conversation.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Russian present-tense verbs take a set of personal endings that show who is doing the action. For a common regular verb such as читать (chitat, to read), the forms are: я читаю (ya chitayu, I read), ты читаешь (ty chitaesh, you read, informal singular), он or она читает (on or ona chitaet, he or she reads), мы читаем (my chitaem, we read), вы читаете (vy chitaete, you read, plural or polite), and они читают (oni chitayut, they read). Notice that each ending - -ю, -ешь, -ет, -ем, -ете, -ют - names a specific person and number. Because the ending already tells you the subject, Russian frequently omits the pronoun, just as Latin and Spanish do. Russian also distinguishes an informal 'you', ты (ty), used with friends and family, from a polite or plural 'you', вы (vy). The present tense is used for actions happening now and for general truths.

sections.heading: Key words & examples
sections.text: The full present of читать (chitat, to read): я читаю (I read), ты читаешь (you read, informal), он читает (he reads), она читает (she reads), мы читаем (we read), вы читаете (you read, polite or plural), они читают (they read). The same endings drive работать (rabotat, to work): я работаю (ya rabotayu, I work), мы работаем (my rabotaem, we work). In a sentence: Я читаю книгу (ya chitayu knigu, I am reading a book); here читаю already means 'I read', so the я is optional. Она работает (ona rabotaet, She works). Они читают по-русски (oni chitayut po-russki, They read in Russian). Say each form and listen to how the ending, not a separate pronoun, carries the person and number of the subject.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Supply the form or translate, then check. 1) What does читают (chitayut) mean? 2) Give 'we read' from читать. 3) Which pronoun, ты or вы, do you use with a close friend? 4) Translate Она работает (ona rabotaet). 5) Why can Russian often drop the pronoun? Answers: 1) 'they read'. 2) мы читаем (my chitaem). 3) ты, the informal singular 'you'. 4) 'She works' or 'She is working'. 5) because the verb ending already shows the person and number of the subject. Read the ending first, and you will know who is acting even before you reach the rest of the sentence.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: using ты with a stranger or an elder; the polite вы is expected until you are invited to be informal. Mistake: forgetting that the ending already names the subject and piling on an unnecessary pronoun in every sentence. Mistake: mixing the endings, for instance saying читаю when you mean читает. Mistake: assuming every verb is perfectly regular; the most common verbs follow the pattern, but some verbs change their stems and must be learned individually. Exit ticket: (a) What does the ending tell you in a Russian present-tense verb? (b) Which 'you', ты or вы, is polite? (c) Give the form of читать for 'they'. Answers: it shows the person and number of the subject; вы is polite; они читают.

items.example: Я пью воду. (ya pyu vodu - I drink water.)
Это хорошая книга. (eto khoroshaya kniga - This is a good book.)
Мой дом здесь. (moy dom zdes - My house is here.)
русский язык (russkiy yazyk - the Russian language)

lessons.title: Russian as a gateway to great literature
lessons.grammar_note: To read a Russian sentence, find the verb, then the nominative subject, then the other endings - the endings, not the order, tell you who does what.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: By the end of this lesson you will be able to put together the pieces of this course - alphabet, pronunciation, gender, case, and verbs - into a simple reading method, and you will understand why so many learners take up Russian to read its literature in the original. Warm-up: you can already sound out Cyrillic and spot a subject and an object; what would it feel like to read a line of Tolstoy as he wrote it? This closing lesson steps back from drills to show where the road leads. The grammar you have met is not an obstacle course; it is the key that unlocks one of the richest literary traditions in the world, along with everyday conversation, travel, and work across a vast region spanning two continents.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: A simple method ties the course together. First, sound out the word in Cyrillic, trusting the letters and placing the stress. Second, find the verb and read its ending to learn the person. Third, find the nominative noun, your subject, and any accusative noun, your object. Fourth, let the other case endings fill in details like possession or location. Because the endings carry the grammar, you can read confidently even when the word order is unfamiliar. As for the bigger reward: Russian is the language of an extraordinary body of literature. Writers such as Pushkin, Tolstoy, Dostoevsky, Chekhov, and Akhmatova wrote in Russian, and translation, however skilled, always leaves something behind - the rhythm, the wordplay, the exact shade of a verb. Many learners press on through the cases precisely so they can one day read these authors in the original, and hear the language as its greatest writers heard it.

sections.heading: Key words & examples
sections.text: Read step by step. Я читаю книгу (ya chitayu knigu): the verb читаю ('I read') already gives the subject, so the sentence means 'I am reading a book', with книгу the accusative object. Она читает по-русски (ona chitaet po-russki) means 'She reads in Russian'. Build up a literary vocabulary too: писатель (pisatel) means writer, книга (kniga) means book, роман (roman) means novel, and стихи (stikhi) means poems or verse. A famous opening, from Tolstoy, begins Все счастливые семьи похожи друг на друга (vse schastlivye semyi pokhozhi drug na druga), 'All happy families are alike' - notice семьи (semyi), the plural of the word for family you met with the soft sign. You can already recognize letters, stress, and a noun in that line, which is no small thing.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Answer, then check. 1) What is the first step when reading a Russian sentence aloud? 2) In Я читаю книгу (ya chitayu knigu), which word is the object? 3) Name two famous writers who wrote in Russian. 4) What does писатель (pisatel) mean? 5) Why do many learners want to read Russian literature in the original rather than in translation? Answers: 1) sound out the Cyrillic and place the stress. 2) книгу, the accusative object. 3) for example Tolstoy and Dostoevsky (Pushkin, Chekhov, and Akhmatova also count). 4) writer. 5) because translation cannot fully carry the rhythm, wordplay, and exact shades of meaning of the original. Keep reading a little every day, and these sentences will steadily open up.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: reading strictly left to right and assuming the first word is the subject; find the verb and the nominative first, then let the endings guide you. Mistake: waiting until your grammar is 'perfect' before touching real Russian - short, simple sentences are worth attempting early. Mistake: leaning only on transliteration; the sooner you read Cyrillic directly, the faster you progress. Mistake: treating literature as out of reach; start with short poems and simple prose. Exit ticket: (a) After sounding out the words, what do you find first in a sentence? (b) Which case marks the subject? (c) Name one great writer who wrote in Russian. Answers: the verb, then the nominative subject; the nominative; for example Tolstoy, Dostoevsky, or Pushkin. The alphabet you learned on day one is the doorway to all of this.
